passages.source_text: εἰ δέ τις τῶν παρεστώτων, διοικεῖν δυνάμενος τὴν ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὑποστέλλεται, τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀναπαύσεως φροντίζων μόνης, καὶ αὐτὸς προσδοκάτω ἀκοῦσαι „δοῦλε πονηρὲ καὶ ὀκνηρέ, ἔδει σε τὸ ἀργύριόν μου προβαλεῖν ἐπὶ τῶν τραπεζιτῶν, καὶ ἐγὼ ἂν ἐλθὼν ἔπραξα τὸ ἐμόν· ἐκβάλετε τὸν ἀχρεῖον δοῦλον εἰς τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον“. καὶ εὐλόγως. σοῦ γὰρ (φησίν), ἄνθρωπε, τοὺς λόγους μου ὡς ἀργύριον ἐπὶ τραπεζιτῶν βαλεῖν καὶ ὡς χρήματα;δοκιμάσαι. τὸ οὖν πλῆθος τῶν πιστῶν δεῖ ἑνί τινι πείθεσθαι, ἵνα οὕτως ἐν ὁμονοίᾳ διατελεῖν δυνηθῇ. τὸ γὰρ εἰς ἀρχὴν μιᾶς λῆγον ἐξουσίας μοναρχίας εἰκόνι τοὺς ὑπείκοντας αἰτίᾳ εὐταξίας εἰρήνης ἀπολαύειν τίθησιν, τὸ δὲ πάντας φιλαρχοῦντας ἑνὶ μόνῳ ὑπεῖξαι μὴ θέλειν, καὶ αἰτίᾳ διαιρέσεως πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν.

ἀλλ᾽ .ἔτι μὴν πειθέτω τὰ παρ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖς γινόμενα πῶς νῦν πολλῶν κατὰ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ὄντων βασιλέων συνεχῶς πόλεμοι γίνονται· ἔχει γὰρ ἕκαστος πρόφασιν εἰς πόλεμον τὴν ἑτέρου ἀρχήν. ἐὰν δὲ εἷς ᾖ τοῦ παντὸς ἡγεμών, οὗ εἵνεκεν πολεμεῖ οὐκ ἔχων αἴδιον τὴν εἰρήνην ἔχει. πέρας γοῦν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς καταξιουμένοις αἰωνίου ζωῆς ἕνα ἐν τῷ τότε αἰῶνι βασιλέα τοῦ παντὸς καθίστησιν, ἵνα αἰτίᾳ μοναρχίας ἄπτωτος εἰρήνη γένηται. χρὴ οὖν ἑνί τινι ὡς ὁδηγῷ τοὺς πάντας ἕπεσθαι, ὡς εἰκόνα θεοῦ προτιμῶντας, τὸν δὲ ὁδηγὸν εἶναι τῆς εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν εἰσούσης εἰσόδου ἐπιστήμονα.

τίνα δὲ ἄλλον αἱρήσομαι τῶν παρόντων ἢ Ζακχαῖον, πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἰσιὼν ἀνεπαύσατο, τοῦ σώζεσθαι κρίνας ἄξιον εἶναι; καὶ τοῦτο εἰπών, παρεστῶτι τῷ Ζακχαίῳ ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα, ἐβιάζετο ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν. ὁ δὲ Ζακχαῖος προσπεσὼν τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτοῦ ἐδέετο ὅπως τοῦ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσῃ, μετὰ τοῦ ὑπισχνεῖσθαι καὶ λέγειν ὅτι Ὁπόσα ποτὲ χρὴ τὸν ἄρχοντα ποιεῖν, ποιήσω, μόνον μοι τὸ ὄνομα τοῦτο μὴ ἔχειν χάρισαι· εὐλαβοῦμαι γὰρ τὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐνδύσασθαι ὄνομα· πικροῦ γὰρ φθόνου καὶ κινδύνου γέμει.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Εἰ τοῦτο εὐλαβῇ, ἄρχων μὲν μὴ καλοῦ, ἀλλὰ ὁ καθεστώς, τοῦτο τοῦ κυρίου δεδωκότος λέγεσθαι τῷ εἰπεῖν „μακάριος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος, ὃν καταστήσει ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ“. εἰ δὲ παντελῶς οὐ θέλεις γνωσθῆναι ὅτι ἐξουσίαν διοικήσεως ἔχεις, ἀγνοεῖν μοι ἔοικας ὅτι ἡ ὁμολογουμένη τοῦ προκαθεζομένου ἐξουσία πολύ τι δύναται πρὸς δυσωπίαν τοῦ πλήθους. ὡς γὰρ εἰληφότι τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἕκαστος πείθεται ὡς μεγάλην ἀνάγκην τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχων. τί δέ; οὐχὶ καὶ ἀσφαλῶς γινώσκεις ὅτι οὐχ ὡς οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχειν ἔχεις, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς δοῦλος (αὐτοῖς ὑπηρετῶν), ὡς πατήρ (ἀδικουμένοις), ὡς ἰατρός (ἐπισκεπτόμενος), ὡς ποιμήν (φυλάσσων), συνελὼν ἐρῶ, τὰς πάσας ὑπὲρ τῆς αὐτῶν σωτηρίας φροντίδας ἔχων; ὅτι οἴει ἀγνοεῖν με οἵους καμάτους ἀναδέξασθαί σε βιάζομαι, ὑπὸ ὄχλων κρίνεσθαί σε ἀξιῶν, οἷς ἀρέσαι τινὰ ἀμήχανον; θεὸν δὲ εὖ πράττοντα πείθειν δυνατώτατον. διὸ δέομαι προθύμως ἀναδέξασθαι, διὰ θεόν, διὰ χριστόν, ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀδελφῶν σωτηρίας, ὑπὲρ τῆς αὐτῶν οἰκονομίας καὶ σῆς ὠφελείας.

καὶ τὸ ἕτερον δὲ λόγισαι ὅτι ὥσπερ κάματον καὶ κίνδυνον ἔχει τὸ τὴν χριστοῦ ἐκκλησίαν οἰκονομεῖν, τοσούτῳ μείζων ὁ μισθός. ἀλλ’ ἔτι μὴν καὶ ἡ κόλασις μείζων τῷ δυναμένῳ καὶ ἀπειθήσαντι. βούλομαι οὖν, πολυμαθέστερον εἰδώς σε τῶν παρεστώτων, δανείζειν καλὰς γνώμας, ἃς παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου πεπίστευσαι, ἵνα „εὖ δοῦλε ἀγαθὲ καὶ πιστὲ“ ἀκούσῃς καὶ μὴ ὥσπερ ὁ τὸ ἓν ἀποκρύψας τάλαντον, ἔγκλημα λαβὼν κολάσει ὑπεύθυνος ἀναφανῇς. εἰ δὲ μὴ βούλει ἀγαθὸς φύλαξ καταστῆναι τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ἕτερον ἀντὶ σοῦ μήνυσον, σοῦ πολυμαθέστερον καὶ πιστότερον. ἀλλὰ οὐ δώσεις. σὺ γὰρ καὶ τῷ κυρίῳ συνῆς καὶ τὰς θαυμασίους πράξεις ἱστόρησας καὶ διοίκησιν ἐκκλησίας μεμάθηκας.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: But if any of those present, though able to manage people’s unreasonableness, draws back, caring only for his own rest, let him too expect to hear, “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my silver before the bankers, and when I came I would have collected what was mine. Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.” And rightly so. “For it was your responsibility,” he says, “human being, to put my words before bankers like silver and to test them like currency.” Therefore, the multitude of believers must obey one particular person, so that in this way it may be able to continue in harmony. For a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority, as an image of monarchy, puts those who submit in a position to enjoy peace because of good order; but when all are eager to rule and unwilling to yield to one alone, they are also certain to fall because of division.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διοικεῖν δυνάμενος τὴν ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: though able to manage people’s unreasonableness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἀγνωμοσύνη denotes deficient judgment or unreasonable conduct; “ingratitude” is lexically possible but fits the governing context less well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Wicked and lazy servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος is rendered “servant”; the context still carries the subordinate status of a servant answerable to his lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would have collected what was mine
lexical_decisions.rationale: πράσσω here means exacting or recovering what is due, rather than merely “doing” what belongs to the speaker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For it was your responsibility, he says, human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive σοῦ with the following infinitives is understood as an elliptical expression of obligation: “it was your part” or “it was your responsibility.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to test them like currency
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκιμάζω evokes testing or assaying currency; “them” refers to the preceding λόγους, though the Greek does not repeat the object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ εἰς ἀρχὴν μιᾶς λῆγον ἐξουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter phrase describes an arrangement or system ending in one governing authority.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as an image of monarchy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative εἰκόνι characterizes the single-authority arrangement as a likeness or representation of monarchy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they are also certain to fall
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχειν with an infinitive expresses what lies ahead or is inevitable; “they must also fall” is a viable alternative.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a Greek question mark between χρήματα and δοκιμάσαι, interrupting two coordinated infinitives. The translation follows the defensible syntactic coordination while disclosing the punctuation rather than treating it as missing wording.

source_issues.source_quote: τὸ δὲ πάντας φιλαρχοῦντας ἑνὶ μόνῳ ὑπεῖξαι μὴ θέλειν, καὶ αἰτίᾳ διαιρέσεως πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν
source_issues.issue: The sentence begins with a neuter substantivized infinitival construction but shifts to the plural finite verb ἔχουσιν, with the semantic plural πάντας supplying the sense. This is intelligible as an anacoluthon, so no restoration is required.

passages.text: But furthermore, let what happens before our eyes persuade us: now, with many kings throughout the whole earth, wars happen continually. For each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war. But if one person is leader of the whole, having nothing for which to wage war, he has perpetual peace. Ultimately, then, for those deemed worthy of eternal life, God appoints one king over the whole in that age, so that, because of monarchy, unfailing peace may come about. Therefore, everyone must follow one person as guide, honoring him as an image of God, while the guide must know the entrance leading into the holy city.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let what happens before our eyes persuade us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb has no expressed object; “us” represents the assembled hearers, while “persuade the observer” or “be persuasive” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχει γὰρ ἕκαστος πρόφασιν εἰς πόλεμον τὴν ἑτέρου ἀρχήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean a pretext, occasion, or stated reason; “pretext” preserves the author’s critical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having nothing for which to wage war
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative expression is understood impersonally as the absent reason or occasion for war; “having no one against whom to wage war” is a contextual alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ultimately, then
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέρας functions adverbially as “at last,” “in the end,” or “as the final outcome,” introducing the eschatological arrangement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unfailing peace
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπτωτος literally describes what does not fall or collapse; “secure peace” or “unshakable peace” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honoring him as an image of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω conveys assigning precedence or special honor; “preferring him” would be more literal but less clear in this context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν εἰσούσης εἰσόδου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the entrance leading into the holy city
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s repeated entrance-and-entering image without reproducing an awkward English cognate construction.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period between the elided ἀλλ᾽ and ἔτι. It appears to be stray editorial punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; no wording has been supplied in its place.

passages.text: “Whom else among those present shall I choose except Zacchaeus, to whom our Lord also went in and rested, judging him worthy to be saved?” After saying this, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus, who was standing there, and pressed him to sit in his chair. But Zacchaeus fell at his feet and begged him to release him from governing, while making this promise and saying, “Whatever a leader must do, I will do; only grant me not to bear this name. For I am wary of putting on the name of office, for it is full of bitter envy and danger.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἰσιὼν ἀνεπαύσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom our Lord also went in and rested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording says that the Lord entered or went in to Zacchaeus and rested; it does not explicitly name a house.

lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him worthy to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive articular infinitive depends on ἄξιον and identifies that of which Zacchaeus was judged worthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐβιάζετο ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν
lexical_decisions.chosen: pressed him to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb can mean compel, constrain, or strongly urge. “Pressed” preserves the insistence without necessarily implying physical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Zacchaeus, though Peter remains a grammatically possible referent; the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: release him from governing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive infinitive names the responsibility from which Zacchaeus asks to be released.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am wary
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may express caution, apprehension, or reverential fear; “I am afraid” is possible but somewhat stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: putting on the name of office
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation retains the clothing image of ἐνδύομαι and renders ἀρχή as governing office in this context.

passages.text: And Peter said, “If this is what you are wary of, do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed,’ since the Lord permitted this expression to be used when he said, ‘Blessed is that man whom his lord will appoint over the care of his fellow servants.’ If, however, you do not want it known at all that you have authority to administer, you seem to me not to realize that the acknowledged authority of the one presiding has considerable power to inspire deference in the multitude. For each person obeys one who has received the authority, since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint. What then? Do you not also know for certain that you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do, but as a servant (ministering to them), as a father (to those being wronged), as a physician (attending to them), as a shepherd (guarding them)—in short, I say, having every concern for their salvation? Do you think I am unaware what sort of toils I am pressing you to undertake when I require you to be judged by crowds whom it is impossible for anyone to please? Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor. Therefore I ask you to undertake it willingly, for God’s sake, for the Messiah’s sake, for the salvation of the brothers, for their proper ordering, and for your benefit.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄρχων μὲν μὴ καλοῦ, ἀλλὰ ὁ καθεστώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed’
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁ καθεστώς is a perfect participial title meaning the person who has been established or appointed, deliberately distinguished from ἄρχων.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since the Lord permitted this expression to be used
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute says that the Lord granted or allowed this designation to be spoken; “gave this to be said” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: over the care of his fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεραπεία can denote care, service, attendance, or a body of attendants. “Over the company of his fellow servants” is therefore possible, but “care” fits the ensuing description of pastoral duties.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος and its compound are rendered with “servant”; the compound stresses shared subordination to the same lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to inspire deference in the multitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπία concerns restraint produced by respect, shame, or awe. “To overawe the multitude” is possible but gives the phrase a harsher tone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μεγάλην ἀνάγκην τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle most naturally continues with ἕκαστος as its subject; conscience supplies the compelling reason to obey recognized authority.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχειν ἔχεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχεις with the infinitive expresses what Zacchaeus is expected or obliged to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you think I am unaware
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial ὅτι introduces an elliptical rhetorical question; “Is it because you think I am unaware?” is a more explicit alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when I require you to be judged by crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀξιόω with an infinitive can mean require, expect, or deem appropriate, rather than necessarily “consider worthy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν δὲ εὖ πράττοντα πείθειν δυνατώτατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person acting well is taken as the subject of πείθειν and God as its object. More literally, “to persuade God” or “to prevail upon God” is possible; context favors the idiom of gaining divine approval.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the Messiah’s sake
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions independently as a title here, so it is rendered “the Messiah” under the supplied policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for their proper ordering
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομία can denote administration, management, arrangement, or stewardship. The genitive may be understood as the proper ordering or administration of the brothers.

passages.text: Also consider this other point: to the degree that administering the Messiah’s church involves toil and danger, the reward is that much greater. But furthermore, the punishment is also greater for one who is capable and disobeys. Therefore, knowing that you are more learned than those present, I want you to lend out the good counsels with which you have been entrusted by the Lord, so that you may hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and not, like the one who hid the single talent, be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation. But if you do not wish to become a good guardian of the church, identify someone else in your place, more learned and more faithful than you. But you will not provide one. For you were with the Lord, gave an account of the marvelous deeds, and learned how to administer a church.

lexical_decisions.chosen: administering the Messiah’s church
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομεῖν denotes managing or administering, and Χριστός is rendered as the independently functioning title “Messiah.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the reward is that much greater
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοσούτῳ supplies the proportional counterpart to the preceding toil and danger: the greater the burden, the greater the reward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for one who is capable and disobeys
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival participles describe someone able to accept the responsibility who nevertheless refuses or disobeys.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to lend out the good counsels
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the financial metaphor of δανείζειν. γνώμαι may also be rendered “teachings,” “judgments,” or “principles.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: with which you have been entrusted by the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive treats the counsels as a trust committed to Zacchaeus by the Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Well done, good and faithful servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The isolated εὖ implies commendation, conventionally expressed in English as “Well done”; δοῦλος follows the supplied “servant” policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔγκλημα is a charge, accusation, or ground of blame, and ἀναφανῇς means being shown or found to occupy the stated condition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: identify someone else in your place
lexical_decisions.rationale: μηνύω here means disclose, point out, or name a suitable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But you will not provide one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is unexpressed but is supplied by the previously requested alternative person; “you will not produce one” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gave an account of the marvelous deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean recount or report what one has learned, supporting the narrative rendering chosen here. In view of the preceding statement that Zacchaeus was with the Lord, the experiential alternatives “observed the marvelous deeds,” “witnessed the marvelous deeds,” or “became acquainted with the marvelous deeds” are also contextually viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the marvelous deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: θαυμασίους may be analyzed as the feminine accusative plural of a two-termination adjective agreeing with πράξεις; the printed form therefore does not require correction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: learned how to administer a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the noun “administration” with “church”; the verbal English form expresses the acquired practical knowledge without adding a new claim.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
